title: [Engineering at Meta] How Meta Uses AI Agents to Scale ML Innovations Across Ads Ranking Models
summary: Our previous post in this series introduced the Ranking Engineer Agent (REA), an autonomous system that generates hypotheses, designs experiments, and proves new machine learning (ML) techniques on ads ranking models. Now, we’re sharing how we propagate ranking model improvements like architectural advancements and training optimizations efficiently across a large and diverse fleet of ads ranking models. This post walks through this process that we call “technique propagation” and how we’re optimizing the process using AI agents. Since agents began driving execution in March 2026, we estimate AI agents handle over 60% of all technique propagation. Measured against the same work before agents, early results show 3x greater engineering productivity, a median 4x reduction in training compute across select combinations, and an estimated $45M+ in compute savings by the end of the year. Meta’s ads recommendation system is powered by a large number of distinct ads ranking models, each serving different product surfaces and advertiser objectives, and each with its own architecture, training data, and serving constraints. Across this portfolio, ML researchers and engineers are continuously advancing the state-of-the-art through innovations we call “techniques.” A technique is anything that makes a ranking model better such as architectural advancements like Wukong factorization layers, Interformer interaction networks, richer data representations, training optimizations, or efficiency improvements in training and inference. However, because each model has its own architecture, data, and training and serving constraints, a technique proven on one model almost never copy-pastes onto the next. At the same time, speed matters because ML techniques have a shelf life. An innovation that delivers gains today may be superseded within a couple of model development cycles. The faster proven techniques reach the full model fleet, the more value they deliver before the next generation of techniques arrive. So how do we propagate a technique to a diverse fleet of models as quickly as possible, while minimizing engineering bandwidth and compute? Scaling Technique Propagation Propagating a growing inventory of proven techniques across a large fleet of diverse models creates a combinatorially expanding space of technique-model combinations to explore, where both engineering bandwidth and compute become significant constraints. The standard way to adapt a technique is to have engineers who are domain experts manually execute adaptation. An engineer studies how a technique interacts with a specific model’s architecture, generalizes it, and tunes it to that model’s constraints. This produces the strongest results, and is still the process for our highest-revenue models, but it does not scale to all of the models in the space. Each adaptation is effort-intensive and demands deep familiarity with both the technique and the target model. So throughput is capped by engineering bandwidth while the opportunity for adaptation grows much faster. The second constraint on propagation is compute. Every adaptation attempt requires a training run, and with a finite compute budget the question is not only which techniques to try but how to navigate the combinatorial space of configurations without spending the budget on attempts (most of which will produce suboptimal gains). Both constraints point to the same requirement: To propagate techniques to a large number of diverse models quickly, propagation has to become standardized, automated, and able to make judgment calls. We started by standardizing model design and automating propagation: a template-driven approach organizes models into a small set of reusable and composable building blocks, so a technique validated once at the template level propagates automatically to every model built from that template. Over the last 2 years, through standardization and automation, we have shipped 5,000+ technique-model combinations across our large, diverse fleet of models while reducing per-model engineering time by 92%. You can read more about it in our post on Standard Model Templates (SMT). Standardization and automation handle the deterministic steps, but successful and efficient propagation still requires making judgment calls, such as which technique is worth propagating to which model, how wide a hyperparameter search should be, why a model is not showing gains, or how to detect and resolve failures. Those decisions still required significant human bandwidth, which prevented us from scaling further and from reaching a state where all techniques reached all applicable models within a few weeks of being proven. That is where AI agents come in. Scaling Technique Propagation With AI Agents Our technique propagation system is built around three capabilities: Discovery: Keep a live view of which techniques have been proven and estimate how well each might transfer to generate a prioritized set of technique-model candidates, ranked by expected impact. Generalization: Generalize a proven technique so it works on models it was not originally designed for. For models built from shared templates, a technique is generalized once per template and reaches every model built from it. Beyond what templates cover, each model needs its own adaptation, which is where the deepest technical reasoning happens. Adoption: Turn validated adaptations into shipped models, many at a time: launching experiments, managing asynchronous multi-day training runs, monitoring convergence, diagnosing and recovering from failures, and assembling proposals that can land. Today, AI agents supercharge all the above capabilities by taking on the judgment-heavy, non-deterministic decision making and bringing deep intelligence to the system. They combine LLM-based reasoning with specialized ML tooling to handle the work of deciding which adaptations to try, diagnosing why something failed and automatically mitigating it, navigating hyperparameter search spaces efficiently, and managing capacity across hundreds of concurrent jobs. The agents share a common knowledge base, an accumulated record of prior training runs, model architectures, and technique outcomes, so they build on what has already been learned rather than starting from scratch. How Agents Speed Up Discovery Discovery answers two questions: What proven techniques exist, and how applicable are they to each model in the model fleet? Until recently, domain experts answered both, working through the assessments one model at a time. They tracked research and results across the organization, spotted the techniques worth propagating, and relied on their domain knowledge to judge applicability. Agents aren’t constrained by the same knowledge or engineering bandwidth limitations as domain experts. Instead of relying on what any one expert knows, they draw on the shared knowledge base, and they make assessments across the entire model fleet at once rather than one model at a time. They systematically identify which proven techniques exist, estimate their transferability across the model fleet, and produce prioritized technique lists ranked by expected impact. Engineers now only have to review the agents’ assessments and make a decision from there. How Agents Make Generalization More Computationally Efficient Generalization is the process of re-implementing a technique proven on one model so it applies to models with different architectures, feature representations, training data, and serving constraints. The core idea usually transfers, but the implementation almost never does. The customization needed depends on the technique and the target model, ranging from retuning hyperparameters, to adapting features to what the target model already consumes or resizing the architecture to fit its inference budget, to redesigning the technique outright. Deciding what a given model needs, and how far to go, is a judgment call. Depending on whether a model is built from standardized templates or customized individually, generalization comes in two flavors, and agents assist with both: Template generalization: For models built from standardized templates, agents assist with building, evaluating, and improving the templates themselves. They propose template optimization hypotheses from proven techniques, launch experiments across representative model sets, evaluate results, diagnose failures, and iterate through multiple rounds, helping manage the multi-day loops that template development requires. Validating a technique once at the template level costs a fraction of the compute of adapting each model separately. Bespoke generalization: For our highest-revenue models, where we still customize a technique for each model, agents progressively learn while working alongside ML engineers during the initial application of a technique to a small number of models. As the engineer makes adaptation decisions such as adjusting configurations, tuning hyperparameters, or resolving failures, the agent tracks every change and outcome, encoding what works, what doesn’t, and which decisions are model-specific versus generalizable. With that grounding, the agent proposes and tests adaptations for the remaining models, with the engineer reviewing and steering rather than driving each one. Drawing on millions of prior training runs and each target model’s own properties, agents start from the configurations most likely to work, use the results of each round of training runs to narrow the hyperparameter search space for the next, and decide which experiments are worth continuing and which to stop early. As a result, when measured across select technique-model combinations, we have seen a median 4x reduction in training compute. How Agents Accelerate Adoption At the adoption stage, agents ship generalized techniques model-by-model. They launch experiments, manage asynchronous multi-day training runs, fine-tune each model, monitor convergence, recover from failures, and assemble validated proposals. Fine-tuning happens differently depending on how the technique arrived. For techniques applied individually, agents help find the best configuration of technique bundles for that particular model. For models built from a shared template, an auto-research loop searches on top of the template, tuning each model for the gains the shared configuration alone does not deliver. When failures occur, whether from an infrastructure issue, training divergence, or a data pipeline error, integrated debugging and recovery diagnose the root cause and apply targeted fixes or retries. Running hundreds of these workflows at once raises the question of which jobs get priority, and which runs are worth continuing or stopping early. Getting the most out of a fixed compute budget is a global optimization problem, and it is where we are currently investing. Agents monitor concurrent training jobs, rank them by revenue importance, technique potential, and deadline proximity, and reclaim capacity from stalled or low-value runs, so GPUs stay pointed at the highest-value work rather than sitting idle or queued behind lower-priority experiments. In the past, an engineer had to watch each run, triage every failure by hand, and restart it, which capped each of them at a handful of models. Now they can keep oversight at the decision points, approving plans and setting priorities at a 3x greater productivity (each engineer can now handle 3x more technique-model adaptations), compressing the time from a proven technique to a shipped model. How We Evaluate Agent-Driven Propagation Techniques propagated by agents are evaluated the same way as those propagated by engineers. A technique has to show improved offline metrics for predictive performance, such as normalized entropy (NE), while not regressing on key guardrails like training or inference cost. It then has to show a statistically significant win in online A/B testing before it can be shipped. But a single evaluation at the end comes too late to steer an agent working across stages over days. Each stage produces a different artifact, so each needs its own metrics. This is how we validate what agents are doing. Discovery: We measure the precision and recall of the technique-model candidates agents select. For a given technique, precision is the share of selected models where the technique ultimately ships, and recall is the share of all viable models for that technique that agents surfaced. Recall matters more here, since a model missed at this stage never gets a second chance; precision acts as a guardrail against spending compute on techniques that will not work. Generalization: We evaluate techniques generalized by agents across a wide range of models to ensure each delivers gains beyond the model it was originally proven on. We first test every generalized technique on scaled-down versions of models, screening technique-model adaptations broadly while keeping compute usage efficient. Then techniques that pass are evaluated on a representative set of full-size models, where they must improve NE and meet every guardrail metric before moving to adoption. Adoption: At this stage, we continue to evaluate correctness with the same predictive performance and guardrail metrics as before. But adoption is also the most operationally heavy stage, with experiments that run for days, so we evaluate agent productivity as well. Two metrics matter most: the number of human interventions needed to complete an experiment, which shows how much engineering time each experiment still takes, and the percentage of issues agents diagnose and mitigate on their own. Humans continue to be key stakeholders throughout the propagation process, reviewing key decisions, confirming judgment calls, and ultimately approving what ships. Making Agent-Driven Propagation the Standard at Meta Given our early results, we are ramping agent-driven workflows to be the primary modality for technique propagation across the model fleet. Today it can take over a year for every proven technique to reach every applicable model. We’re aiming to reduce that time down to three months. Achieving that means pushing agent-driven workflows toward 5x higher end-to-end throughput, so propagation keeps pace with innovation rather than trailing it. To get there we are continuing to invest in the intelligence of the agents themselves, improving the quality of generalization, capacity efficiency, and execution through self-evolving learning, where agents refine their own strategies based on accumulated outcomes rather than relying solely on human-provided heuristics. Propagating techniques across the models is one component of a larger vision. We are agentifying every aspect of the end-to-end model development lifecycle across the ranking AI space, from exploration and hypothesis generation to propagation, experimentation, and production launch. These agents represent the scaling layer of this system, ensuring that every proven innovation reaches its full potential across the model fleet. title: [Kubernetes] Announcing the Workload Conformance Working Group
summary: We are excited to announce that the Kubernetes community now has a Workload Conformance Working Group. The working group is writing a shared standard for how workloads behave at runtime on Kubernetes. To get it right, we need input from the people who build those workloads and from the people who run the clusters they're deployed on. Why workloads need a shared standardCertified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade. The problems they find are familiar. A routine node drain is often how you discover that an application can't tolerate disruption. An upgrade can break an application that still depends on a removed API version. Others show up in day-to-day operation: workloads that ask for privileges they don't need, or reserve resources they never use. Kubernetes already documents much of this, including security and handling disruptions. Even so, every cluster operator ends up repeating the same assessment, and application maintainers get the same questions from each environment they support. A common specification with repeatable tests would give both groups the same baseline to start from. What the working group will deliverThe charter sets out three deliverables: A specification of workload behavior for each Kubernetes minor version. A method for testing each requirement against a running workload. Upstream conformance tooling that implements those tests. The first step is deciding which workloads and behaviors the specification covers. The scope includes security, resilience during disruptions, resource use, networking, storage, API usage, and observability, but the group hasn't yet agreed on specific requirements or on how to test them. However, one rule is already set: every requirement needs an objective test that a test binary can run, so nothing subjective goes into the specification. The specification covers how a workload runs, and importantly not what it does. Consequently, application logic is out of scope of workload conformance. The binary won't retest anything Certified Kubernetes already covers, and it won't require a particular workload packaging format, or vendor tool like policy engine, security scanner, etc. How the work is organizedTwo Special Interest Groups (SIGs) are sponsors for the working group. SIG Architecture will own the specification and tooling through a subproject, which will be created once the first artifacts are proposed by the Working Group. SIG Apps will bring the application perspective. Whenever a requirement touches another Kubernetes SIG's area, such as node behavior or networking, the working group will initiate conversations with those SIGs as well. The working group is a forum where SIGs can get involved and shape the direction of Workload Conformance while the specification is being written. We're aiming for a stable first specification and working tests within two to three Kubernetes release cycles. Get involvedThe specification will and needs to be built from real examples, so we want to hear your experiences. If you run clusters, tell us how you assess workloads today and what broke during your last upgrade or maintenance window. If you maintain an application, tell us what it needs from the cluster and where the existing guidance left you guessing. Beyond examples, the work needs reviewers for proposed requirements and contributors to write the tests and tooling. When early versions of the tests are ready, we also want early testers to run the binary against your own workloads and tell us where the results differ between runs or environments. If a requirement touches your SIG's area, help us check its scope and the test behind it. And because the subproject will outlive the working group, we're also looking for people who want to maintain it for the long term. You can find us in #wg-workload-conformance on Kubernetes Slack (visit slack.k8s.io for an invitation) and on the mailing list. The working group meets every other Wednesday at 15:00 UTC. The Zoom link and the agenda are in the meeting notes. If you want to raise a topic, add it to the agenda. Joining the mailing list usually adds the meeting invite to your calendar. Thanks to everyone who reviewed and supported the working group proposal.

title: [Kubernetes] Why Is My Kubernetes Job Still Pending? Tracing Kueue Admission with Headlamp
summary: You submit a Kubernetes Job and wait for its Pods to appear. A minute passes. Then another. The Job is still suspended, there are no application logs, and there may not even be a Pod to inspect. In a cluster managed by Kueue, this can be completely normal. Kueue may still be deciding whether the Job can use the requested resources. The useful question is not only “Why is the Pod pending?” It is first “Has Kueue admitted the Workload?” The Kueue plugin for Headlamp brings that investigation into the Headlamp UI. Instead of reconstructing the admission path from several commands and large YAML objects, you can begin with the Workload, read its condition message, and follow links through the LocalQueue, ClusterQueue, ResourceFlavor, and Cohort. This article follows that Headlamp-first path. The command line appears only in a short optional section for reproducing the example. Before you beginYou need a Kubernetes cluster with Kueue installed, a Headlamp installation, and the 0.1.0-alpha Kueue plugin. Your Kubernetes identity must be allowed to read the Kueue resources used in this article. The alpha release provides read-only views for Kueue v1beta2 Cohorts, ClusterQueues, LocalQueues, ResourceFlavors, and Workloads. It does not add its own create, edit, stop, resume, or delete workflows. Headlamp still provides its standard YAML and resource actions where your permissions allow them. First, separate admission from Pod schedulingKueue and the Kubernetes scheduler answer different questions. Kueue admission: Should this Workload start now, considering queue policy, quota, ResourceFlavors, admission checks, and other waiting Workloads? Pod scheduling: After the Workload is admitted and the Job resumes, which nodes can run its Pods? That boundary changes the investigation. If the Workload is not admitted, stay in the Kueue section of Headlamp. If it is admitted but its Pods are still Pending, move to Headlamp's normal Job and Pod views and inspect scheduler events. Kueue admission architecture The Headlamp-first troubleshooting pathThe quickest investigation starts with the Workload, not with a shell. Tracing a pending Job through Headlamp Step 1: Open the Workloads viewIn Headlamp, open Kueue → Workloads. Select the namespace that contains the Job, then find the Workload created for it. Kueue creates a Workload to represent the resource request and admission state of a Job. In the alpha plugin, owner references are shown as Kind/name text but are not yet clickable. The Workload name normally contains the Job name, so the namespace filter and table search are the simplest ways to locate it. Before opening the detail page, the list already gives you a useful first scan: LocalQueue priority and priority class active state admitted state completion state a readable current status such as Admitted, Finished, or Inadmissible age If there is no matching Workload, check three things before going further: the selected namespace, whether the Job was submitted to a LocalQueue, and whether your Kubernetes account can list Workloads. The plugin performs permission checks and displays an access message when the current identity cannot read a resource. Step 2: Read status, conditions, and eventsOpen the Workload. Start with its current status and conditions, not with the full YAML. For admission troubleshooting, the most important condition types are QuotaReserved and Admitted. Admitted=True means Kueue has admitted the Workload. The Job can resume, so any remaining Pending Pods belong to the scheduling branch of the investigation. QuotaReserved=False with a reason such as Pending means Kueue has not reserved quota. The condition message explains what prevented the reservation. An Inadmissible status means the Workload currently cannot fit the available queue configuration. A missing covered resource, unsuitable ResourceFlavor, stopped queue, or admission check can all lead you here. For example, a condition message may report that Kueue could not assign a ResourceFlavor because the ClusterQueue has insufficient CPU quota. That message is the first real answer to “Why is my Job still pending?” The rest of the Headlamp journey explains the configuration behind it. Also check the Events section. Conditions describe the current state; events help show what recently changed or what Kueue attempted. Step 3: Compare the Workload's request with its assignmentStay on the Workload detail page and inspect the PodSets and resource requests. The plugin shows the requested Pod count, CPU, memory, and other resources that Kueue evaluates together. This matters because a Job with parallelism: 3 and a one-CPU request per Pod asks Kueue for three CPUs in total. Looking at only one Pod's template would underestimate the Workload. If quota has already been reserved, the same page also shows the assigned ClusterQueue, ResourceFlavors, and admitted resource usage. If those admission assignments are absent, the Workload has not reached that point yet. In our example, the Workload requests: three Pods three CPUs in total 600 MiB of memory in total The next question is where that request entered Kueue. Step 4: Follow the linked LocalQueueUse the LocalQueue link on the Workload detail page. A LocalQueue is the namespace-level entry point used by the Job. It connects namespaced Workloads to a cluster-scoped ClusterQueue. The LocalQueue page shows: its namespace and connected ClusterQueue stop policy and current status pending, reserving, and admitted Workload counts Kueue conditions and Kubernetes events related Workloads in the same namespace This page answers two practical questions: Did the Job enter the queue you expected, and is it the only Workload waiting there? If the LocalQueue is inactive or stopped, that may already explain the wait. If it is active, follow the linked ClusterQueue to inspect the capacity behind it. Step 5: Inspect ClusterQueue capacity and usageA ClusterQueue represents the cluster-level quota and admission policy available to one or more LocalQueues. On its Headlamp detail page, compare the Workload request with: covered resources nominal quota for each ResourceFlavor current reservations and usage borrowing and lending limits pending, reserving, and admitted Workload counts queueing strategy and stop policy preemption, fair-sharing, flavor-fungibility, and admission-check settings Kueue conditions and Kubernetes events For the example in this article, the ClusterQueue provides a nominal quota of two CPUs and two Pod slots. The Workload asks for three of each. The condition message and the ClusterQueue page now tell the same story: the Workload does not fit, so Kueue leaves the Job suspended. This is an admission-capacity problem. It is not evidence that kube-scheduler failed to find a node. Step 6: Check ResourceFlavor and Cohort when neededQuota is not always a single pool. A ResourceFlavor can represent a class of compute through node labels, taints, tolerations, or topology settings. Use the ResourceFlavor link from the ClusterQueue when the condition mentions flavor assignment or when the Workload requires a particular hardware class, such as GPU nodes. If the ClusterQueue belongs to a Cohort, follow that link too. Cohorts let ClusterQueues share unused quota. The Headlamp page shows parent and child Cohorts, member ClusterQueues, referenced ResourceFlavors, resource groups, borrowing and lending limits, and fair-sharing information. These pages help answer a more subtle question: Is the Workload blocked because the queue has no quota of its own, because it cannot borrow enough, or because no suitable flavor can be assigned? What we learned without leaving HeadlampFor the sample pending Job, the UI gives us a complete explanation: The Workload is not admitted. Its QuotaReserved condition is false and the message points to insufficient quota. The Workload requests three CPUs and three Pod slots. Its LocalQueue is active and points to the expected ClusterQueue. The ClusterQueue provides only two CPUs and two Pod slots. Kueue therefore keeps the Job suspended until quota becomes available or the queue configuration changes. The important part is not that Headlamp invents a new status. It reads the same Kubernetes API objects as other clients, then places the related resources and human-readable values in one connected investigation. If the Workload is admitted, switch viewsSuppose the Workload detail page shows Admitted=True, but the application is still not running. Kueue has completed its part of the decision. Continue in Headlamp's standard Kubernetes views: Open Workloads → Jobs and inspect the Job state and events. Open Workloads → Pods and filter by the Job name or namespace. Select a Pending Pod and read its Events section. At this stage, look for scheduler concerns such as insufficient node capacity, node affinity, taints and tolerations, topology constraints, persistent-volume binding, or image-pull failures. This handoff is the most useful troubleshooting rule in the article: Not admitted: investigate Kueue resources in Headlamp. Admitted, but Pods are Pending: investigate Job, Pod, node, and scheduler information in Headlamp. A repeatable Headlamp checklistWhen the next Job does not start, use this short path: Open Kueue → Workloads and select the correct namespace. Find the Workload associated with the Job. Check the readable status, Admitted, and QuotaReserved conditions. Read the condition message and recent events. Compare PodSet resource requests with any admission assignments. Follow the LocalQueue link and confirm its status and ClusterQueue. Follow the ClusterQueue link and compare quota, reservations, usage, and policy. Inspect ResourceFlavor or Cohort details when the message points to flavor selection or shared quota. If admitted, move to Headlamp's Job and Pod views. What Headlamp replaces during this investigationThe plugin does not replace kubectl or kueuectl for scripts, exact object output, or changes. It replaces the repetitive UI-less navigation needed during an interactive investigation. Question Headlamp path Command-line equivalent Is the Workload admitted? Kueue → Workloads → status and conditions kubectl describe workload <workload-name> -n <namespace> Which LocalQueue did it enter? Workload → linked LocalQueue kubectl get localqueue <localqueue-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml Which ClusterQueue provides quota? LocalQueue → linked ClusterQueue kubectl get clusterqueue <clusterqueue-name> -o yaml Which flavor or shared quota matters? ClusterQueue → ResourceFlavor or Cohort kubectl get resourceflavor <flavor-name> -o yaml or kubectl get cohort <cohort-name> -o yaml What happened after admission? Workloads → Jobs and Pods → events kubectl describe job <job-name> -n <namespace> or kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> For scripts and GitOps workflows, the command line remains the right tool. For a person asking “why is this waiting?”, the linked Headlamp path is usually faster to read. Optional: reproduce the pending scenarioThe plugin repository includes sample Cohort, ClusterQueue, LocalQueue, ResourceFlavor, and Job manifests for local testing. Apply those examples to a cluster where Kueue is installed, then open the Kueue section in Headlamp. To reproduce the specific quota mismatch used in this article, configure a ClusterQueue with two CPUs and two Pod slots, then submit a three-Pod Job that requests one CPU per Pod. The Job enters its LocalQueue, Kueue creates a Workload, and the Workload remains pending because the combined request is larger than the available quota. Keeping this setup separate from the main walkthrough is intentional: once the resources exist, the investigation itself should happen in Headlamp. Current alpha limitationsThe 0.1.0-alpha release is an initial read-only view of the Kueue admission path. The plugin does not add its own create, edit, pause, resume, or delete flows. Workload owner references are displayed as text and are not currently navigable. The UI depends on the Kubernetes permissions of the identity used by Headlamp. Metrics and a visual relationship map are possible follow-up areas rather than features of this release. These limits are useful to state clearly: the plugin's current purpose is to make admission state and resource relationships easier to inspect. Developed during LFX MentorshipThe plugin was developed during CNCF LFX Mentorship 2026 Term 2 using TypeScript, React, Kubernetes APIs, and Headlamp's plugin system. Utkarsh Raj implemented the plugin with guidance and review from René Dudfield (@illume) and Kevin Hannon (@kannon92). Feedback from the Headlamp and Kueue communities shaped the resource views, status presentation, navigation, documentation, tests, and first alpha release. Try it and share feedbackExplore the plugin source and README, read the 0.1.0-alpha release documentation, or share feedback in the release issue. If a pending Workload is still difficult to explain after following the Headlamp path, that is exactly the kind of feedback that can improve the plugin.

title: [CNCF] 🚀 The story behind “Drone 2”: My KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 keynote
summary: An open source adventure featuring Kubernetes, agent-substrate, kagent, AI agents, drones, and more! Just 30 seconds before going live for the KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2026 closing keynote, “Cloud Native Without Limits: What Can AI Agents Do for Us?”, while Abdel Sghiouar was introducing me, Cory Jett leaned over and whispered: “The drone isn’t connecting to the controller!” 😱 A heart-stopping moment! Thankfully, a quick reboot saved the day. And then came the moment I’ll never forget: walking onto the stage with a live drone following right behind me! 🚁✨ And when I finally walked off stage, all the nervousness and anxiety were gone. I was just SO happy! What a feeling! ❤️ On-stage live demo with the drone and big screens 🥋 From Amsterdam to Salt Lake City: Never give up! After my Amsterdam keynote, where the drone camera failed, Christian Dussol taught me the martial arts lesson of “Osu” (never give up! 🥋💪). That lesson stuck with me, and I wanted to push the boundaries even further in Salt Lake City. Striking the “Osu” posture after the Amsterdam keynote While brainstorming with Allison Price around our theme, “Cloud Native Without Limits,” we asked ourselves: What if we could let the audience experience what it’s like to fly and build something live on stage, powered by AI agents? Of course, bringing a live drone indoors isn’t exactly plug-and-play. There was quite a bit of work behind the scenes! 🛠️ Behind the scenes: Making the impossible possible A few challenges we had to tackle: 🛩️ Regulatory compliance: Back in August, we learned that an FAA Part 107-certified remote pilot was required for our indoor drone operation. Cory stepped up, completed the necessary training in just one week, and saved the demo! 🙌 Teaser at the venue 😅 🏠 Home testing: I got propeller guards so I could safely experiment with code, test flight paths, and practice flying indoors at home. Let’s just say my house became a mini drone testing lab! Flight testing at home with propeller guards But this demo was about much more than flying a drone. We wanted to show what real-time agentic execution looks like, with the right guardrails, sandboxing, and observability in place. 🤖 Under the hood: The Cloud Native technologies behind the drone Here’s what powered the experience: 🤖 Agents: Running on CNCF Sanbox projects agent-substrate, and kagent providing an opinionated layer for building and running agents. 🔐Then AAIF Growth project agentgateway: Playing multiple roles: LLM gateway: Rate limiting and controlling access to models. Egress gateway (as part of agent-substrate): Enforcing sandbox and network access policies. MCP gateway: Handling authentication and authorization for Model Context Protocol tool calls with an Identity Provider, for example, Keycloak. 📊 OpenTelemetry and Jaeger: Providing end-to-end observability across agent execution through agentgateway and agent-substrate, including rate-limiting errors, the duration of each tool call, and where agents spend most of their time. All coming together to make an AI-powered physical experience happen, live on stage! The moment when it all comes together live on stage 💜 A big Thank You & what’s next? 🇪🇸 The community’s response was incredible! It’s exciting to see how far we’ve come as an industry, bringing AI models, agentic AI, and cloud native technologies together to make things possible that would have seemed like science fiction just a few years ago. A massive THANK YOU to my manager, Idit Levine, for her unwavering support; Cory Jett, for making the drone flight possible; Allison Price, for brainstorming this adventure with me; Jonathan Bryce, for loving the drone idea when I casually brought it up during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2025; Elna Vogel, for making sure we had the required insurance. And of course, a huge shout-out to the entire event and technical teams who helped bring this adventure to life! ❤️ Last but definitely not least, THANK YOU to the agent-substrate, kagent, and agentgateway communities! They answered every question I threw at them, responded incredibly quickly, and were always ready to jump in and debug live if needed. I couldn’t have pulled this off without you! 💜 My #substrate-dev team CNCF slack 📺 Missed the keynote? Catch the full recording! Now, I’m officially wrapping up the Drone 2 chapter and already looking forward to building something fresh for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon 2027 in Barcelona! 🇪🇸 So, what physical objects or hardware should we hack on next? Drones have had their moment. What’s next? What could we build that I haven’t even imagined yet? 🙂

title: [Cloudflare] Introducing Search for Agents
summary: AI Search, our service that indexes your content and lets you add search to any application or agent without having to build an entire retrieval infrastructure, has supported adding your website as a data source for a while now, automatically crawling, converting and indexing its pages.Still, setting up an AI Search instance for your website requires manually creating and configuring it initially, and then doing all the integration work to get the search endpoints available from your domain and to make sure that agents know where to find the index and know how to use it.Today we're introducing Search for Agents, which puts that setup behind a toggle in your Cloudflare dashboard. Turn it on for your zone, and our service will create your AI Search instance, start indexing your content, and make search discoverable and available from your own domain.How it worksThe idea follows naturally from Markdown for Agents, where Cloudflare's network converts any HTML page to Markdown in real time for enabled zones using content negotiation headers. Similarly, Search for Agents leverages the power of AI Search by automatically creating an index for your zone and exposing APIs that any AI agent can discover and use to search your website, under your domain, all done at the network level.You can enable Search for Agents using the API, or by going to the dashboard in your zone page, under Quick Actions:Search for Agents is available to all customers, including Free (with limits). Once it’s enabled, Cloudflare will automatically create an AI Search instance, start crawling and indexing the content in your zone. Refer to our developer documentation to understand how the crawling process works.You can access your instance directly from this page, or by going to directly to your account’s AI > AI Search instances view:The AI Search instance for your zone is created with default settings, but you can enable reranking or change configuration options like cache settings at any time. Refer to our documentation for the full list of options.Once AI Search indexes your content, you or any agent on the Internet can start using Search for Agents, subject to your domain settings (e.g. your bot management settings, AI Crawl Control and web application firewall (WAF) configurations).DiscoverabilitySearch isn't much use if the agents don’t know it's there. To facilitate discoverability, Search for Agents automatically advertises the search endpoint on every page of your site.For example, for HTML responses, we add metadata to the page's <head>:<meta name="agent:instructions" content="Use this search API to find relevant content across this site with keywords or natural-language queries, instead of crawling individual pages. Results are returned in Markdown."> <meta name="agent:endpoint" content="https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search?q={query}"> <meta name="agent:method" content="GET"> <meta name="agent:documentation" content="https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai-search/how-to/search-for-agents/">If you also have Markdown for Agents enabled, an agent requesting a page with Accept: text/markdown receives the same information in YAML front matter:--- agent: instructions: "Use this search API to find relevant content across this site with keywords or natural-language queries, instead of crawling individual pages. Results are returned in Markdown." endpoint: "https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search?q={query}" method: "GET" documentation: "https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai-search/how-to/search-for-agents/" ---The agent will easily pick up these instructions and know what to do next to search your site.Searching contentOnce the agent knows that your site has a search endpoint, it can start using it:$ curl "https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search?q=cloudflare+artifacts" # Search results for: "cloudflare artifacts" ## docs/artifacts/api/workers-binding/index.md (score: 1.000) # Workers binding · Artifacts · Cloudflare Artifacts docs Call Artifacts from a Worker binding. --- ## docs/artifacts/index.md (score: 0.951) # Artifacts · Cloudflare Artifacts docs Store, version, and share filesystem artifacts across Workers, APIs, and Git-compatible tools. ...Depending on your AI Search configuration, the agent can also use natural language and ask questions to the search endpoint:$ curl --get "https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search" --data-urlencode "q=What is the maximum push size for Cloudflare Artifacts?" # Search results for: "What is the maximum push size for Cloudflare Artifacts?" ## docs/artifacts/platform/limits/index.limits-cloudflare-artifacts-docs.md (score: 1.000) # Limits · Cloudflare Artifacts docs Section: Limits · Cloudflare Artifacts docs title: Limits description: Review Artifacts platform limits. pcx_content_type: reference products: - artifacts Limits that apply to creating, importing, cloning, and pushing Artifacts are detailed below. These limits cover naming rules, storage, request rates for control-plane and Git operations, and the size of each push. FeatureLimitControl-plane request rate2,000 requests per 10 seconds per Artifacts namespaceGit request rate, per artifact2,000 requests per 10 seconds per artifactMaximum storage per repository1 GB for repos created on or after 2026-09-29. Repos created earlier have a 10 GB limit. See size limit change.Maximum storage per account1 TB (can be raised on request)Maximum number of repositoriesUnlimitedMaximum number of namespacesUnlimitedNamespace name length2–63 charactersNamespace and repo namesStart with a letter or digit. Remaining characters may include letters, digits, ., _, and -.Maximum push size64 MiB per push. Includes all data sent in the push. Split larger work into several smaller pushes.Maximum objects per push50,000 objects, such as file versions, folders, and commits.Maximum file size32 MiB per file. Already-compressed files, like images, video, or zip archives, may be rejected slightly below 32 MiB.Maximum ref updates per push1 MiB of branch and tag updates per push.Maximum entries per folder100,000 files and subfolders in a single folder. ...Note that this search endpoint returns retrieved content, in Markdown, not a generated answer. The agent already has an AI model and a conversation with the user; all it needs is the relevant information from your site, not another AI model's attempt to answer on its behalf.Supporting a new HTTP method: QUERYThe new HTTP QUERY method is an IETF Proposed Standard, incidentally coauthored by our own James Snell, published in June 2026 as RFC 10008. A QUERY allows a client to send search criteria in a request body safely and idempotently without modifying server state. This makes it a good fit for AI search.The adoption of QUERY is underway with major browser vendors discussing the RFC and multiple frameworks and clients either adopting (curl and undici, for example), or discussing adoption.Search for Agents supports QUERY natively either using a plain text or JSON request body:# Plain text curl -X QUERY 'https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search' \ --data 'What is the maximum payload size per ingestion request in Basin Pipelines?' # JSON curl -X QUERY 'https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search' \ --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \ --data '{"q":"How many bulk import requests per minute does Email Service allow?"}'See it in actionLet’s see it in action during an agentic session. Search for Agents is enabled for our Developer Documentation. When we open an OpenCode session and ask “What is the maximum push size for Cloudflare Artifacts?”, in the logs we can see the agent discovering the search endpoint on the homepage and then fetching /.well-known/search with the question for the search results.The answer comes back a few seconds later and it’s correct.Once the agent discovers the search API, it will likely reuse it multiple times within the same session whenever it needs to search for content in the same site.We enabled Search for Agents for our developer documentation ahead of this announcement and we’ve found that agents do a good job of discovering the search API and using it during their tasks.It’s still an AI Search instanceBecause Search for Agents is powered by an AI Search instance in your account, you get all the standard configuration options and features as well. For example, you can enable public REST API or MCP endpoints, or use it from Workers, or even embed AI Search on your website for human visitors.Start using Search for AgentsStarting today, Search for Agents is available to all customers. The usage follows the AI Search pricing; that includes ingesting content, storing the index's content, and serving queries, subject to the account's included usage and limits for both the Workers Free and Paid plans.We also recommend you check our Agent Readiness page (see announcement) and understand how you can make your sites optimized for agents, from guiding agents on how to authenticate, to controlling what content agents can see, the format they receive it in, and how they pay for it.Check out the Search for Agents developer docs for more information. Follow us on X or come and talk to us in the Cloudflare Developer Discord. We'd like to hear from site owners making their content searchable to agents.

title: [Microsoft Azure] Microsoft and Oracle bring agentic AI into flow of enterprise work
summary: This blog is co-authored by Arpan Shah, SVP of Oracle Databases and Muneer Mirza, VP of Multicloud at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). Today at Microsoft Ignite, we’re bringing agentic AI into the flow of enterprise work. Our new integrations let AI agents reason across Oracle’s business-critical data—from finance and supply chain to HR and customer operations—and the work context Microsoft Work IQ understands across meetings, email, documents, and Teams. Customers can access this combined intelligence through Excel, Teams, and Microsoft Copilot. Built on Oracle AI Database@Azure, the integrations help businesses turn trusted enterprise data into insights and actions, with the choice, security, and performance mission-critical workloads demand. Learn more about Oracle on Azure With Oracle AI Database@Azure, Oracle and Microsoft have helped customers modernize critical workloads to improve application performance and unlock more value from their enterprise data, by bringing databases closer to applications and connecting enterprise data with Microsoft AI. Oracle AI Database@Azure now spans 33 Azure regions, more than on any other hyperscaler, delivering the performance and flexibility customers need. At Oracle AI World 2026, we announced new capabilities for Oracle AI Database@Azure including FedRAMP Class D certification coming soon for US Government and public-sector workloads, and Proximity Placement Groups (PPGs) that enable customers to place their database closer to applications—resulting in approximately 50% lower VM-to-Exadata network round-trip latency than deployments without PPG alignment. Now, at Microsoft Ignite 2026, we’re building on that momentum. For IT operations: Monitoring and trust at every layer Today, we’re announcing limited preview of Azure Workload Center for Oracle, bringing each workload’s architecture, resources, and dependencies together through a construct called a Workload Virtual Instance (WVI). This significantly reduces the complexity and resources required to manage solutions at the individual component level. Integrations across the Workload Virtual Instance, Azure Monitor Health Models, and the Microsoft Azure Copilot Run Oracle agent connect monitoring signals across application, database, and infrastructure layers. This operational visibility is complemented by agent access controls: Oracle AI Database@Azure supports Microsoft Entra authentication and Oracle Deep Data Security, helping agents stay within users’ existing permissions while database calls run through the managed model context protocol (MCP) server and activity remains auditable across your Oracle database estate. For example, after business users report poor performance from an order processing application, an admin must quickly diagnose and fix the problem. The admin signs in with their existing Microsoft Entra identity and uses Azure Workload Center for Oracle to get a unified view of workload health including signals across the infrastructure, database, and application layers while Copilot provides a summary highlighting where to focus. The admin uses a natural-language prompt to initiate a coordinated investigation involving multiple agents, each with Oracle data access limited by their identify profile. Database calls from the agents run through the managed MCP server, and every action is captured for audit. Working together, the agents synthesize their findings into a single operational conclusion for the admin. For end users: Oracle data in the flow of work Business users need insights from Oracle data, but they often need assistance from someone more technical to extract, format, and deliver it. The new Oracle AI Database plug-in for Excel, available today, lets users connect Excel directly to Oracle Database, pull trusted data into the worksheet, and reason over it with Copilot without leaving the spreadsheet. No export, no manual preparation, no ticket to IT. Together, Microsoft and Oracle are bringing intelligence to the workflows that run the business: giving analysts, planners and controllers the power to understand margin changes, analyze shifts in demand, resolve reconciliation issues, and act on supply chain disruptions. Copilot analyzes Oracle transaction data and enriches it with context from Work IQ, drawn from meetings, email, documents and Teams, to identify exceptions, draft an explanation, and prepare a governed action plan for review. Rather than another dashboard, or disconnected chatbot, this is AI in the flow of work, grounded in systems of record maintained in Oracle AI Database. For developers: Build trusted agents quickly, from prototype to production Pilots are easy; production is hard. Real processes span multiple data sources, call for several specialized agents, and demand answers a business can stand behind. Developers can build agents that connect to Oracle AI Database using Microsoft Foundry with Managed Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and A2A protocol. MCP servers enable governed access from Azure agents to Oracle AI Database, whether it runs in Oracle Cloud Infrastructure or as Oracle AI Database@Azure, through approved SQL and PL/SQL operations, tools, and predefined reports. Application roles determine which tools each user or group can use, so agents never reach beyond what IT has sanctioned, and AI comes to the data rather than the data being copied out to AI. These integrations make Oracle AI Database a first-class source of knowledge, memory, and data for agents built in Microsoft Foundry. For example, a developer builds a sales intelligence application involving an agent retrieving account and order data from Oracle AI Database through MCP, a product agent identifying cross-sell opportunities, and a finance agent weighing in on account health. Through coordinated activity across these agents, the sales intelligence team receives a concise sales brief through an API. In another scenario, a customer service agent, grounded through Foundry IQ, can answer questions about a policy or an account with supporting citations, and recall the customer history from Oracle-backed memory, retrieve similar past interactions, and responds with context. And watch the Oracle Theater on-demand session THRSP1082 for more information on Azure Workload Center for Oracle. title: [Microsoft Azure] Azure Cobalt 200 VMs now available, proven on real workloads and built for the agentic era
summary: Today at Microsoft Ignite 2026, we’re announcing the general availability of Azure Cobalt 200-based virtual machines (VMs). Cobalt 200 VMs deliver up to 50% better performance than Cobalt 100 and are now available in 14 regions, expanding to 23 regions by the end of 2026. Built for cloud-native, data-intensive, and agentic AI workloads, Cobalt 200 VMs will represent a significant share of new Azure Compute capacity beginning in 2027. Explore Cobalt 200 VM sizes and deployment guidance For customers like Amadeus, Databricks, InMobi, OpenAI, and Snowflake, Cobalt 200 VMs deliver improved performance and efficiency over Cobalt 100 VMs. As a result, customers can deliver faster search results, more responsive database queries, and run their services at higher utilization with fewer cores. Cobalt 200 VMs deliver up to 50% better performance than Cobalt 100 Read the blog › Cobalt 200’s performance and efficiency gains reflect our systems approach to infrastructure design, which co-optimizes silicon, software, networking, power, and rack infrastructure. Cobalt 200 VMs are also designed for agentic AI workflows, including agent sandboxes, file search, code compilation, and tool execution, where higher per-core performance can help reduce latency. As customer need for high-performance and low-latency compute increases, we’re adding new virtual machine types to bring the price-performance benefits of Cobalt to additional workloads: Mpsv4 for high memory workloads. Lpsv5 for workloads needing fast access to large datasets. With Microsoft Azure Boost included in every Cobalt 200 VM, customers get the latest accelerated network and remote storage performance in Microsoft Azure. Proven on critical customer workloads Our benchmarking for Cobalt 200 VMs showed significant performance increases for a wide variety of workloads. We observed up to 1.5 times increased performance for web serving workloads, up to 1.6 times for Java-based workloads, up to 1.5 times for AI agent tool execution workloads, and 1.9 times for database workloads over Cobalt 100. We’ve seen these results translate into real-world improvements as our customers bring Cobalt 200 VMs to their own workloads. Ubuntu Pro keeps those systems patched and supported for the long term. On Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, that includes Kernel Livepatch, which applies high and critical kernel fixes on Arm-based VMs without a reboot. —Cindy Goldberg, VP, Cloud and Silicon Partnerships, Canonical Improving efficiency at Microsoft scale Microsoft products and services, including Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure DevOps, Azure SQL, Microsoft 365, XBOX, and more, run on Cobalt VMs for increased performance, improved efficiency, and cost savings at scale. Accelerating cloud database workloads Cobalt 200 was designed to deliver high-performance for database workloads, and at Microsoft Build 2026, we announced the availability of Azure Database for PostgreSQL on Cobalt 200. Cobalt 200 VMs provide scalable performance, memory capacity, and local storage needed to accelerate Azure Database for PostgreSQL. Advancing custom silicon development Microsoft’s silicon engineers run EDA workloads for design verification, physical implementation, and sign-off, and they benchmarked many of those workloads on Cobalt 200 VMs. The team reported increased performance and efficiency with Cobalt 200, with performance between 1.3 and 4.15 times over Cobalt 100. The increased performance allows the team to run more test cases in the same amount of time, supporting the development of more advanced Maia and Cobalt silicon. Speeding up developer workflows Every second counts when developers are waiting on a build. Cobalt 200 VMs allow GitHub Actions larger Arm runners to finish jobs noticeably faster than on Cobalt 100. Across the millions of workflows run every day, those gains add up to faster feedback for developers and more efficient use of compute. Gaming XBOX evaluated Cobalt 200 VMs on its web service and caching layer, the behind-the-scenes building blocks that help players sign in, see what their friends are playing and jump into games more quickly. Running natively on Arm, XBOX achieved improved performance and efficiency compared to their current infrastructure, a jump that matters in gaming for delivering fast and reliable gameplay. Scaling media processing The media processing service running video for Microsoft Teams observed 1.65 times the performance on Cobalt 200 compared with Cobalt 100, allowing them to further optimize their capacity needs to serve customers. Testing also showed linear scaling across Cobalt 200 physical cores, with vCPU utilization reaching up to 90% while serving traffic. Compute designed for agents, powered by custom systems Modern AI applications have evolved from simple inference-based chat interfaces to complex reasoning and agentic systems requiring high-performance compute infrastructure paired with AI acceleration. Cobalt 200 is optimized from the lowest levels of the silicon to the overall rack and system architecture for the demands of agentic compute. Azure Cobalt 200 server board At the center of every Cobalt 200 VM is the Cobalt 200 system-on-chip (SoC). Built on TSMC’s advanced 3nm process technology to deliver optimal performance and efficiency, the Cobalt 200 SoC brings together 132 Arm Neoverse V3 cores, with a multi-chipset architecture, and advanced packaging. Compute: Each vCPU is a full physical core, with 3MB of private L2 cache, and 192 MB of system-level cache, helping provide consistent performance under load while keeping recently accessed data close to the core. Memory: Cobalt 200 features a custom memory controller with 12 channels of DDR5 and enables memory encryption by default with negligible latency. Networking and storage: Cobalt 200 VMs include the latest version of Azure Boost, moving networking and storage processing off the host, delivering up to 15% higher network bandwidth, 20% higher remote storage IOPS, and 10% higher remote storage throughput compared with Cobalt 100. Security: Every Cobalt 200 server includes the Azure Integrated HSM which protects the server hardware from unauthorized intrusion and enables protected encryption key storage for hosted workloads. Acceleration: Integrated compression and cryptography accelerators enable Microsoft workloads to reduce CPU consumption by offloading common tasks to specialized low-power silicon. On-chip accelerators will help reduce Azure SQL backup times by up to 2.5 times while minimizing disruption to the live workload. Expanding choice and control Predictable performance or peak performance. Cobalt 200 VMs support two processor modes. Deterministic Mode runs cores at a consistent 3.2 GHz. Opportunistic Mode can boost cores up to 3.6 GHz when power and thermal headroom allow—delivering up to 12% more performance at the expense of some frequency variability. Different customers have different needs. Deterministic Mode suits distributed data and analytics clusters which run at the pace of their slowest node, and services with tight performance targets. Opportunistic Mode suits web and API services, transaction processing, and media workloads, where speed matters more than consistency. Use the ProcessorMode setting to choose deterministic or opportunistic mode when you create a VM or later through the Azure portal, Microsoft Azure CLI, PowerShell, or Azure Resource Manager and Biceptemplates. Cobalt 200 VMs are available in five VM series, across general purpose, memory-optimized, high-memory, and storage-optimized families. Cobalt 200 adds two new VM families for Arm-based compute on Azure: High-memory Mpsv4—with 16 GiB of memory per vCPU for large in-memory databases, ERP systems, large caches, and memory-intensive analytics. title: [Docker] Meet the New Docker: Built to Run on Trust
summary: Evolving an iconic brand for the agentic era Today, Docker is officially launching its new brand, and I’m excited to tell you what it’s all about and why we think now is the time for change. Let’s start with the big picture. We’re living through a transformative moment: for Docker, for developers, for the industry, and quite possibly, for humanity itself. AI is creating possibilities that would have sounded like science fiction not long ago. But it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control? Or, put more simply: how do we get to a point where we can actually trust agents? That one seemingly simple yet infinitely complex question is why we’re here today, introducing you to a new Docker. A new Docker, but a familiar story. We’ve been here before Ok, not exactly here, but once upon a time, a decade or so ago, the tech industry was at a similar inflection point. Digital transformation was the term du jour, promising a new way of engaging customers and powering the global economy. There was one big constraint, though: teams needed a better way to build, ship, and run software consistently across any environment. Enter a company you might have heard of: Docker. Together with all of you, Docker built the standard trusted by millions of developers. For over a decade, developers have relied on us to make software portable, open, reproducible, and secure. Docker turned the frustration of “Well, it works on my machine!” into the assurance that “Yes, it works everywhere.” Today, of course, the challenge confronting us is new and evolving, and we all need to evolve with it. We cannot simply continue to do what we’ve always done and expect to succeed in this new era. That applies to business leaders, developers, tech companies, everyone. It certainly applies to Docker. That’s what this rebrand is about: evolving to meet the moment for our customers. What isn’t changing Let me be unequivocal: this is not about leaving Docker’s legacy or heritage behind. We’ve spent more than a decade earning your trust. This is about building on that foundation, not replacing it. The qualities you value us for aren’t changing. We’re still committed to openness and industry collaboration. We’re still, and always will be, developer-first. We’re still fanatical about simplicity, and about showing up everywhere you need us. On the product front, the containers you know and love aren’t going anywhere. Containers still play a huge role in the software development lifecycle. As long as that’s the case, Docker will continue leading the way. Containers weren’t designed for agents Agents have introduced a new problem. Containers isolate workloads. But agents aren’t workloads. Agents are actors. Agents make their own decisions about what to run, what to access, and what to change. Developers and enterprises need solutions built specifically to isolate and govern them, so they can give those agents real autonomy without giving up control. Docker’s next chapter is about delivering exactly that: security, isolation, and governance, so we can all trust agents to do meaningful work without feeling like we’re always one step from catastrophe. Run on trust In case I haven’t made it blindingly obvious yet, the new Docker is all about trust. Trust Docker because our track record speaks for itself. Trust Docker because we’re proven, neutral, and secure. Trust Docker because it’s pretty darn clear you can’t trust the agents to manage themselves. Trust us because we have a software supply chain that is already the standard for building securely. Trust us because nobody isolates agents where they run better than we do. Trust us because we’re taking a comprehensive approach to improving governance and minimizing risk across the entire enterprise. Trust Docker because we’re not egotistical enough to think we can solve a challenge this big alone. Trust us because everything about our history, our heritage, and our actions over the past year tells you we’ll partner with the smartest and build alongside the best, and not create vendor lock-in. Most of all, trust Docker because we’re not just talking the talk. We’ve got the goods to back it up: trusted supply chain for your agents to build from, trusted runtime to isolate your agents, and a trusted ecosystem to ensure all the layers of trust are covered, whether made by Docker or not. A whale of an evolution As our product team innovated to meet the moment and our messaging in the market began to shift, one thing became clear: the speed and scale of evolution happening inside Docker called for an equally momentous evolution on the outside. Something that makes it unmistakably clear that it’s a new day for Docker. Something that says and shows, loud and clear, for all the world to see, that Docker is not just about containers anymore. Something big. Something, dare I say, whale sized. I’m talking, of course, about our beloved Moby. If you know Docker, then you know Moby, and if Docker is evolving, Moby should too. The only question was to how and to what extent? We looked at a lot of whales, folks. (I may or may not have been seeing whales in my sleep.) Ultimately, with the help of our friends at the strategic brand transformation company, Motto, we landed on a new Moby for the new Docker. Watch Moby’s transformation here: In many ways, Moby is a microcosm for Docker and the changes we’re making: the Moby you love and trust, evolved for a new era. Just as the new Docker is no longer singularly defined by containers, neither is the new Moby. Come take a look around We’ve got lots to show you. Poke around our new website. Find and engage with the new Docker brand on social media. And if you want to see what trust in the agentic era looks like in practice, try Docker Sandboxes and Docker AI Governance. We’d love to hear what you think. Wherever this new era takes us, Docker will always honor and cherish the trust you continue to place in us. Now, let’s go build what’s next.

title: [Docker] Give sandboxed agents live web access with the Firecrawl kit for Docker Sandboxes
summary: Sandboxed agents cannot read the web A coding agent in Docker Sandboxes runs inside an isolated VM, the sandbox controls which hosts it can reach, and credentials stay on the host behind a proxy. The same controls keep the agent from opening a docs page, reading a changelog, or looking up an API that shipped after its training cutoff, so it writes code against the version it remembers. The usual fix is to widen the allowlist until the agent can fetch anything, which hands back most of what the sandbox took away. The Firecrawl kit gives the agent web search, page scraping, and site crawling through one added host, api.firecrawl.dev, and every page comes back as clean markdown. In this post, you’ll learn: How the Firecrawl sandbox kit plugs into a sandbox you already run How to install the sandbox kit and give your agent its first live-web task How to check that the SDK, the API key, and the network rule all work What the sandbox kit can’t do yet, and what new work it makes possible for your agent Why a kit The Firecrawl kit is a mixin (kind: mixin): it extends whichever workload you already run rather than defining a new sandbox. Its descriptor, firecrawl/firecrawl.yaml, declares four typed capabilities: An install step (lifecycle@1). It installs the Firecrawl Python SDK, firecrawl-py, pinned to 4.44.0, as the agent user, and fails sandbox creation if the install or import check fails. A credential (credential@1). It requests a proxy-managed firecrawl API key. Inside the sandbox, FIRECRAWL_API_KEY holds the placeholder proxy-managed; the proxy swaps in the real key on requests to api.firecrawl.dev, so the key never enters the image or the sandbox. Network permissions (network-policy@1), split by phase. The install step may reach pypi.org and files.pythonhosted.org; at runtime the agent may reach api.firecrawl.dev. Agent instructions (agent-context@1). A context file tells the agent the capability exists, how to call it, and which limits come from the sandbox. The workload indexes it from its own AGENTS.md. The kit adds to the sandbox’s allowlist and does not narrow it, so everything else is set by your global sbx policy. Docker’s balanced preset allows package registries, GitHub, and a curated list of vendor domains, and returns a 403 for general websites, including most documentation sites, so Firecrawl is the agent’s route to those. Under deny-all, it is the agent’s only web host. Kits are experimental and in Early Access, so the kit format and sbx commands may change. The steps below are current for October 2026; the repository README carries the latest. The workflow Prerequisites The sbx CLI, version 0.46 or later, signed in with sbx login. On macOS: brew trust docker/tap && brew install docker/tap/sbx. Docker Desktop is not required. A global network policy, set once with sbx policy init balanced. Without it, no sandbox starts. A Firecrawl API key (fc-...) from firecrawl.dev/app/api-keys. A workload to add the kit to. This walkthrough uses Docker’s shell workload, docker/sbx-kit-shell, with the Claude Code mixin, docker/sbx-kit-claude-mixin. Other workloads and agent mixins are on Docker Hub. Kit: docker.io/firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl:1.0.0 on Docker Hub, for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. Source: github.com/firecrawl/firecrawl-docker-sandbox. 1. Store the key once on the host. The command prompts for the key. Service secrets are global by default, so every sandbox that requests the firecrawl service can use it once you approve. The kit never sees the value; the proxy injects it at request time. sbx secret set firecrawl sbx secret ls 2. Start a sandbox with the kit. The kit is an ordinary OCI image with its descriptor in the manifest, so a version tag is all you need. Each --kit adds a mixin to the workload, and the trailing . mounts your project directory. sbx run docker/sbx-kit-shell:1.0.0 \ --kit docker/sbx-kit-claude-mixin:2.1.285 \ --kit docker.io/firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl:1.0.0 . On the first run, sbx asks you to approve sending the firecrawl credential to api.firecrawl.dev. Accept the defaults. The credential is required: with no secret stored, sbx refuses to create the sandbox instead of letting the agent hit a 401 mid-task. A detached or CI run cannot answer the approval prompt, so approve interactively once or write the binding to ~/.config/sbx/credentials.yaml first. 3. Give the agent a task that needs the live web. Documentation sites are blocked under balanced, so this one has to go through Firecrawl. Read <https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/changelog/> and list what changed in the latest Pydantic release. Quote the page, don't answer from memory. The kit’s instructions tell the agent to scrape blocked hosts through Firecrawl, so it calls fc.scrape(...) unprompted. Its response, trimmed: The most recent release listed on the changelog is v2.13.4 (2026-05-06). I fetched the page live through Firecrawl. Quoted from the page: > ## v2.13.4 (2026-05-06) > ### What's Changed > #### Packaging > - Bump libc from 0.2.155 to 0.2.185 by @Viicos in #13109 > - Adapt `pydantic-core` linker flags on macOS by @washingtoneg and @Viicos in #13147 > #### Fixes > - Preserve `RootModel` core metadata by @Viicos in #13129 It's a small patch release with no new features. 4. Verify each layer. In the same session, ! runs shell commands inside the sandbox. !python3 -c "import firecrawl, importlib.metadata as m; print('firecrawl-py', m.version('firecrawl-py'))" Expected: firecrawl-py 4.44.0. !env | grep FIRECRAWL_API_KEY Expected: FIRECRAWL_API_KEY=proxy-managed. A real fc-... value here means the key came from somewhere other than the kit. !python3 - <<'PY' from firecrawl import Firecrawl fc = Firecrawl() doc = fc.scrape("<https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/changelog/>", formats=) print(doc.markdown) PY Expected: the page as markdown, starting with # Changelog and the latest version heading. The same URL returns a 403 to curl from inside the sandbox, so output here proves the SDK, the credential, and the network rule at once. The kit also describes itself inside the sandbox. This prints the published descriptor, and the agent instructions sit next to it as firecrawl-context.md: !cat /usr/share/sandbox/kit/firecrawl/kit.yaml Running from source. To review or modify the kit before you run it, clone the repository and point --kit at the firecrawl/ directory; sbx builds source kits on demand: git clone <https://github.com/firecrawl/firecrawl-docker-sandbox.git> sbx run docker/sbx-kit-shell:1.0.0 --kit ./firecrawl-docker-sandbox/firecrawl . Known limitations Under balanced, general websites return a proxy 403 to curl, so a URL found in a scrape result has to be scraped through Firecrawl too. Screenshot and other media formats return links on Firecrawl’s storage host, which the allowlist does not include, so those files cannot be downloaded inside the sandbox. Under organization governance, managed policy overrides the kit’s allow rule, and scrapes fail with a proxy-side 403 until the organization allows api.firecrawl.dev. An HTTP 402 means the Firecrawl account is out of credits; the agent is told to stop rather than retry. What this unlocks With the kit installed, the agent can look things up on the web while it works. The sandbox only needs to talk to one new address, api.firecrawl.dev, and Firecrawl fetches the pages for it. This matters because the default balanced policy blocks most documentation sites. Without the kit, you’d have to allow each site one by one, and every new site you allow makes the sandbox a little less locked down. Without the kit, you had a choice to make. The default balanced policy blocks most documentation sites, so you could either leave the agent working from what it remembered, or allow sites one by one and loosen the sandbox a little each time. The kit avoids that choice. Your Firecrawl API key stays on your machine, behind the proxy, and the agent still reads the web as it is today. Here’s what the agent can do: Code against the current API, not the remembered one. Before calling a library or SaaS API, the agent scrapes its reference page and changelog. It uses today’s parameter names and spots deprecations that shipped after its training cutoff. Upgrade dependencies with the release notes in hand. Asked to bump a package, the agent reads the release notes for every version in between, lists the breaking changes, and edits the code to match before running the tests. Load a vendor’s docs into context. For a new integration, the agent crawls the relevant section of the vendor’s docs and gets it back as markdown, so it can work from the whole guide rather than one page. Research an error it can’t explain. When a build or test fails with an unfamiliar message, the agent searches for it, reads the matching GitHub issue or forum thread, and applies the documented fix or workaround. Cite its sources. Because every answer comes from a fetched page, the agent can quote the text and link the URL it used, so you can check its work. The result is fewer made-up APIs, fewer failed upgrades, and less time spent correcting an agent that was confidently out of date. Where the kit comes from The kit is published under the firecrawl organization on Docker Hub as firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl, with source, changelog, and CI on GitHub under Apache-2.0. The SDK pin is verified against PyPI’s package hashes at install time, and every release passes Docker’s kit-tck conformance suite in CI. Review the descriptor and allowlist before running it, as with any kit. Try it Pull the kit from Docker Hub: hub.docker.com/r/firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl. Issues and feature requests go to the GitHub repository.
